tagline: Mountain ridgelines, forests and a chain of western Maine lakes
intro: The Rangeley Lakes Scenic Byway follows Appalachian ridgelines before descending into hills and valleys in western Maine. The National Scenic Byway Foundation lists its 2000 national designation under recreation, highlighting forests, mountain streams, farm fields and linked lakes and ponds. An archived Federal Highway Administration guide allows two to three hours to drive it and eight or more to visit.

In the 1860s, anglers from eastern cities discovered brook trout weighing 10 to 12 pounds in the region. As word spread, sportsmen and their families began returning annually, traveling by train, buckboard and steamship. Travel here changed with the vehicles that brought visitors. The Phillips and Rangeley Railroad opened in 1891, carrying timber to market and bringing tourists from eastern cities. With the railroad’s end, the automobile and an expanding road network helped shift vacations toward personal camps. The big hotels declined; the Rangeley Lake House was demolished in 1958.

Begin north of Byron on Route 17 and travel north toward Oquossoc. Height of Land gives a view across the lakes region to the mountains beyond, beside the Appalachian Trail. From Oquossoc, follow the lake east toward Rangeley, then turn south on Route 4 to Smalls Falls. The Appalachian Trail crosses both Routes 17 and 4.

moments.title: Height of Land
moments.text: Height of Land puts the Rangeley Lakes region and the mountains beyond into one view. The overlook lies on the Route 17 portion of the byway, before Oquossoc when traveling north, and borders the Appalachian Trail. Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust places its Byway Ambassadors here on summer weekends. Their work includes helping visitors find trails and places to look for moose.
moments.notice: The overlook takes in the Rangeley Lakes region and mountains beyond.

moments.title: Rangeley
moments.text: A ten-mile road was part of Squire James Rangeley’s plan for an estate here. Arriving in 1825, he tried to establish an English system of landlords and tenants, built a sawmill, gristmill and two-story mansion, and connected his property to the outside world by road. He stayed 15 years before selling and moving to Portland. Logging became a principal industry, with steamboats towing log booms across the lakes before river drives carried them onward. A sign in town marks another kind of position: halfway between the Equator and North Pole.

moments.title: Smalls Falls
moments.text: Smalls Falls breaks the Sandy River’s descent into four steps, with pools separating them. Together the waterfalls and cascades drop 54 feet. From the top, the sequence is a 12-foot slide and horsetail, a 25-foot segmented waterfall, a 14-foot horsetail and a three-foot cascade. The falls lie in Township E in western Franklin County. A Route 4 rest area provides access and includes parking and picnic tables.
moments.notice: Pools separate the four drops of Smalls Falls.
